title: Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London
description: Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO heavyweight world title against the man he dethroned Fabio Wardley in a rematch on 17 October in London.
fullText:
Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO heavyweight world title against former champion Fabio Wardley in a highly anticipated rematch on 17 October at London's O2 Arena.

Londoner Dubois, 28, dethroned Wardley with an 11th-round stoppage in a thrilling all-British showdown in Manchester in May to become a two-time world champion.

It was announced during Saturday's undercard of Moses Itauma's IBF heavyweight world title fight with Filip Hrgovic, with Dubois and Wardley facing off in the ring.

Dubois said he is predicting a "dominant victory" before adding: "Let's get it on. It's just a war.

"When you get in the water, you're going to get wet. We will see. Give me some of that face-to-face - boy."

The first meeting lived up to its billing, with two of the division's biggest punchers producing a dramatic fight that showcased the power of both men.

Wardley dropped Dubois twice early in the contest, but a bloodied Wardley absorbed heavy punishment before the referee stopped the bout.

It was the first defeat of the 31-year-old's professional career in his 22nd bout.

"It didn't take long at all [to agree]. The O2 is like a home away from home for me," Fabio Wardley said on DAZN.

"Looking forward to getting straight back into it. Going to be a rematch and going to be revenge.

"We came into the fight with all the confidence in the world, but adjustments needed to be made."

The Ipswich fighter's rise through the sport has been remarkable. Having only taken up boxing at the age of 19, he progressed through the unlicensed white-collar scene before reaching the top of the heavyweight division.

Dubois, meanwhile, has experienced the full spectrum of boxing's highs and lows.

The 26-fight veteran has suffered three defeats during his career but rebuilt himself to claim world honours twice, with his victory over Wardley marking the latest chapter in his comeback story.

The winner of the rematch could be in line for a blockbuster fight next summer against fellow Briton Itauma, provided the heavyweight prospect secures a world title of his own.

The winner of the contest between Itauma and Hrgovic will be required to face mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez.

Should Itauma - who is aiming to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion in history after Mike Tyson - come through both fights, promoter Frank Warren has suggested a potential Wembley Stadium clash with the winner of Dubois-Wardley II next summer.

The heavyweight division remains fragmented following Oleksandr Usyk's decision to vacate his titles. Russian Murat Gassiev currently holds the WBA belt, while Germany's Agit Kabayel is the WBC champion.

title: Dem House hopeful’s delayed disclosure reveals mystery payments from Soros-linked groups
description: Rebecca Cooke's financial disclosure reveals she was compensated by two organizations with direct ties to George Soros' Open Society Foundation.
fullText:
A waitress running for Congress in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District was on the payroll of two left-leaning organizations with ties to billionaire investor George Soros' Open Society Foundation.

Rebecca Cooke has portrayed herself as a working-class outsider, touting her experience as a waitress, small business owner and nonprofit leader raised on a dairy farm.

But a personal financial disclosure released two days after Wisconsin's Aug. 13 primary shows she received more than $5,000 apiece for work with Third Way and the Pipeline Fund, two left-leaning organizations with financial ties to George Soros' Open Society network.

Democratic Group Launches $15M War On Dsa After Socialist Primary Wins: 'Mortal Danger'

The Open Society network awarded $1 million to Third Way's nonprofit research arm between 2023 and 2024, while the Pipeline Fund received $1.4 million directly from the Open Society Action Fund in 2024.

Through the Open Society Foundation, which serves as the umbrella organization for Soros' philanthropy network, Soros has distributed tens of millions of dollars to nonprofits and groups championing left-leaning causes like policing reform, LGBTQ rights and drug decriminalization.

Soros has donated more than $32 billion of his personal fortune to the Open Society's Foundation, which has been overseen by his son Alex Soros since 2022.

The financial disclosure forms only report that the amount of money Cooke received from each organization was above $5,000, but they do not specify the exact amount. The personal financial disclosure form covered Jan. 1, 2025, through July 14, 2026.

A spokesperson for Third Way confirmed with Fox News Digital reporting by The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Cooke received $30,000 in payment "for a project focused on elevating the voices and concerns of working-class Americans that have too often been missing from the rooms where decisions are made."

The Foundation to Promote Open Society, a grant-making arm of George Soros' Open Society Foundations network, donated a $500,000 grant to the Third Way Institute in 2023 and another one in 2024, according to IRS-derived grant records.

Third Way Institute serves as the 501(c) research arm of the Third Way. In 2024, Third Way Institute transferred $21.9 million to Third Way, accounting for roughly 98% of the institute's total spending that year. The institute said the money was used to support charitable and educational work on economic, national security, energy and social policy issues.

Soros Network Rebuilds Progressive Prosecutor Push After String Of Election Losses

Fox News Digital reached out to Third Way for comment.

Pipeline Fund is an organization that works to train, recruit and support progressive candidates running in state and local election races. It began operating independently in 2024 after spinning off from the Sixteen Thirty Fund, a liberal nonprofit network that has received tens of millions of dollars from the Soros-founded Open Society network.

Tax records also show that the Pipeline Fund received $1.4 million directly from the Open Society Action Fund and approximately $2.26 million from the Sixteen Thirty Fund in 2024.

Scattered across the country, Pipeline Fund has a network of campaign consulting groups, including one in Wisconsin known as Wisconsin Progress.

"We can confirm Rebecca Cooke worked as a contractor for The Pipeline Fund in 2025 to help advance our mission of building a reflective democracy where working-class people, women, people of color and other underrepresented communities are fully supported to run for office and advance the needs of their communities," Pipeline Fund said in an emailed statement to The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

House Democrats' Campaign Arm Draws Progressive Fury For Trying To 'Tip The Scales' In Key House Primary

Prior to making a bid for Congress herself, Cooke opened up her own Democratic campaign consulting firm in 2015 and worked with eight state and federal campaigns from 2015 to 2021.

"Radical Rebecca Cooke is a paid political operative for far-left liberals and wants to push their socialist agenda. Commie Cooke may fit in at [a] Soros-funded consulting firm, but she is far too extreme to represent western Wisconsin," National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Zach Bannon said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Cooke's personal financial disclosure was not released until two days after the Aug. 13 primary after an extension she requested from the clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives in April.

All candidates who spend or raise more than $5,000 for a House of Representatives race must submit a personal financial disclosure form 30 days before the election.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., blasted Cooke's delay in releasing her financial records, saying it tells voters all they need to know about her.

"For months, Democrats and Republicans across the 3rd District called on Cooke to release her financial disclosures. She had every opportunity to be transparent with voters. Instead, she chose to keep them hidden until after the primary," Van Orden said in a news release.

Democrat Establishment Strikes Back As Socialist Candidate Downed In Battleground Primary

"That tells Wisconsin voters everything they need to know about Rebecca Cooke's character. She was willing to deceive her own party to protect the political persona she built and gain political power."

But Cooke said her financial forms reveal that she truly is a working-class American.

"I've always worn multiple hats to make ends meet and, in addition to waitressing, I worked on two projects related to getting more working class people to run for office and conducted research for an organization about how to better connect with working class voters," Cooke said in an email to the Sentinel.

"There are unique challenges to running for office as a working class person with an hourly wage job and a full-time campaign schedule. For example, I'm one of the thousands of people in this district who can't afford health insurance. I've been proud to help make it easier for the next generation of working class leaders to step up and take our fight to Washington D.C."

Fox News Digital reached to Open Society Foundation, Cooke's campaign and Pipeline Fund for comment.

title: A Ukrainian air-defense sergeant says missiles aren't his most challenging shortage. It's the gear that finds enemy targets.
description: Ukraine uses MANPADS to down Russian drones, jets, and aircraft, but to be effective, teams need batteries and ways to find targets.
fullText:
A Ukrainian sergeant said supporting gear is harder to get for his air defense unit than missiles.

It uses MANPADS that down Russian jets and aircraft, but needs batteries and ways to find targets.

Equipment like drone detectors and electronic warfare systems is "hard to get," he said.

The hardest shortage facing one Ukrainian shoulder-fired air-defense unit isn't necessarily missiles, its battery sergeant told Business Insider. It's some of the equipment that helps crews find targets and keep their systems running.

The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, serves in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS, which fire shoulder-launched missiles able to engage low-flying aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and drones.

Weapons like these, which include the US Stinger, Polish Piorun, and Soviet-designed Igla, have been a key part of Ukraine's short-range air defense in front-line areas, protecting troops and operations from attacks.

Yankee said that for him, at least, one of the hardest things "is finding resources. Secondary resources, not the weaponry, but electronic warfare stuff."

He said some of the devices that help his team detect threats and keep its equipment working are "hard to get." What is hardest to find is "mostly electronics."

"I'm talking more about devices that locate the drones and warn you," Yankee said. "I'm talking about stuff like EcoFlows, batteries, big batteries, because we have a shortage of them, just in general, just a mass shortage."

Ukrainian soldiers are increasingly using drone detectors, including small handheld or vehicle-mounted models, to warn of certain incoming enemy drones by detecting their radio frequencies.

EcoFlows are portable power stations that can power or recharge essential gear such as radios and communications equipment, Starlink terminals, laptops and tablets, drone equipment, electronic warfare systems, and sensors.

These, and batteries in general, are especially important because soldiers are often far from power outlets, and Russian attacks often shut down energy infrastructure. Running a portable generator would be much louder and might reveal their positions.

Electronic warfare systems are also vital for Ukraine as it tries to disrupt Russia's communications and jam its drones.

Despite their importance, this equipment isn't always easy for units to obtain in sufficient quantities. Some of the gear is much newer and less readily available than supplies like ammunition. And while demand is high, some equipment still isn't being produced in large quantities. In some cases, there are also distribution bottlenecks that affect availability.

Unlike many Western militaries, Ukraine's military doesn't have a highly centralized system for weapons procurement. Units often buy or receive gear themselves, including through crowdfunding.

There are advantages to this setup for rapid innovation because units engage manufacturers directly, but the system can also result in uneven distribution, leaving some units facing shortages.

Ukrainian foundations, units, and other groups that are involved in sourcing and crowdfunding equipment for troops often ask for gear like batteries and detectors, with some describing them as items that air defenders regularly need.

MANPADS and the units that operate them are important for Ukraine. Units, service members, and officials have reported missiles taking down Russian drones, helicopters, and aircraft, and Western analysts have credited MANPADS with making penetrating low-altitude Russian fixed-wing and helicopter sorties too costly for Russia to continue.

A report last year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, said that Ukraine's integration of MANPADS operators into its air defense teams forced Russian pilots to choose between flying high and being targeted by ground-based air defenses or flying low and facing MANPAD missiles. These short-range defenses relieved the pressure on Ukraine's ground-based systems, allowing them to "survive and eventually recover."

Yankee's unit provides air defense for infantry who need to get to the zero line, the far edge of the front line, and, as a result, "we participate in battle," he said.

He said that conditions there can be so dangerous that moving just 300 meters can take 7 days of waiting for safe conditions and protection. Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death."

Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program that trains and equips Ukrainian forces, including at a purpose-built camp in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics, combining Western practices with his existing battle-won skills before returning to Ukraine.

Yankee said he uses the Stinger and Igla systems. Ukrainian soldiers have, at times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, reported shortages of MANPADS missiles, saying those shortages allowed Russian forces to be bolder because they knew the Ukrainians couldn't try to stop as many of their attacks.

But Ukraine's military has not suffered critical shortages of them the way it has with larger, surface-to-air missiles, and allies have announced new deliveries throughout the war.

Not everything is consistent across the force though. Ukraine's military disseminates weapons and ammunition according to operational need, so one unit could be well supplied for critical missions while another comes up short.

title: Dubois beats Moore to keep Baumgardner in picture
description: Caroline Dubois coasts to victory over Amelia Moore in Birmingham to defend her WBC and WBO lightweight titles and stay on course for a blockbuster meeting with Alycia Baumgardner.
fullText:
Caroline Dubois coasted to victory over Amelia Moore to defend her WBC and WBO lightweight titles and stay on course for a blockbuster meeting with unified super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner in 2027.

Dubois dominated the fight at BP Pulse Arena in Birmingham and knocked Moore down in the fifth round but was unable to find the decisive blow against the dogged American.

The British fighter won on unanimous judges' decision - 99-90 99-90 98-91 on the scorecards.

Dubois was heavy favourite for this fight and never looked less than in control, although her reliance on power and presence rather than speed ensured it went the distance to a long, inevitable conclusion.

She sent Moore to the canvas with a booming left in round five, but Moore got straight back up and was instead moved around the ring by Dubois like a cat playing with a mouse.

After the fight, Dubois had a war of words with the watching Baumgardner, who is moving up to lightweight to face IBF champion Elif Nur Turhan in November, accusing the Briton of "tightening up" and being "tired".

Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight

In just her fifth professional fight, Moore - who has two American national championships from a respectable amateur career - showed admirable guts, but lacked the quality to trouble her foe.

It was clear that Dubois has boxed 70 more professional rounds than Moore, and she made light of being four inches shorter to avoid any danger.

Now it is anticipated that Dubois, unbeaten in 15 professional fights with 14 wins, will face Baumgardner next year - should the American beat Turhan.

Dubois and Baumgardner - who both gave separate media conferences promoting their respective upcoming fights in Birmingham on Thursday - have been sniping at each other for a year.

And it continued ringside post-fight, with Baumgardner present for what she called a "scouting mission" on Dubois on Saturday night.

Dubois' new MVP-curated personality - brash and self-confident - was on display as she called out Baumgardner for stepping into "my division - I am the best here", in an expletive-infused exchange.

She has also made changes outside ring, including a shock decision to switch trainer.

Dubois dropped Shane McGuigan in London, who helped guide her to two world titles in the lightweight division, and has opted to make the move to Los Angeles to work with renowned US trainer Manny Robles as she aims to take her career to the next level.

Baumgardner has said she "absolutely" wants to fight Dubois, and if the 32-year-old successfully steps up to lightweight and claims the IBF title in Texas on 8 November, then they should headline another MVP showcase of women's boxing.

Earlier on the undercard, Terri Harper - who lost on points to Dubois in April - began her rebuild with a comprehensive victory against Miranda Reyes which she described as "one of the best performances of my career".

Harper considered retirement after losing to Sandy Ryan in 2024, but had no such thoughts after defeat by Dubois.

And she stepped up to welterweight to take on Reyes, knowing this was a must-win bout to maintain her career as a top-rated fighter as she attempts to win a world title in a fourth weight class.

Harper bounced into the ring with bright yellow gloves, and there was nothing mellow as she continued that energy into the first round - holding the centre of the ring for the majority and landing some good body shots on Reyes.

She then upped her game and brought an early close at the start of the second round, dropping Reyes twice in short order.

A flurry of body shots was followed by a short left hook to down the Houston fighter, and the referee called it off 47 seconds into the second round to the delight of Harper's similarly yellow-attired corner.

"One of the best performances of my career, I'm very happy with that," Harper said. "You can't get rid of me this easily!

"I am excited for what's next. It's way too early [to say goodbye] - I've got a lot to give yet."

It is the seventh knockout win of Harper's career from 17 victories in 22 bouts, and she will now look up again after a timely reminder of her capabilities.

title: Wall Street used to worry that too much U.S. debt would crowd out the private sector. But AI hyperscalers are ‘reverse crowding’ the Treasury
description: "Capital flowing into corporate bonds is capital not flowing into Treasuries, and Treasury yields have had to rise to clear the market."
fullText:
Among the many potential downsides for letting the national debt get too high was that the federal government would suck up so much capital that businesses wouldn't be left with enough.

Today, U.S. debt is at $40 trillion, the federal budget deficit is on track to reach $2 trillion this fiscal year, and debt servicing costs alone are $1 trillion a year.

That's a lot money that the Treasury Department has to raise from the bond market, which is also a key source of financing for corporate giants.

But AI hyperscalers, so far, are still able to issue plenty of their own debt in the mad dash to buy chips, build data centers and lay down other infrastructure.

In fact, even Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has billed himself as America's top bond salesman, has noted the eagerness with which AI companies are offering debt—no matter the cost of borrowing.

"We are also seeing big corporate issuance. And a lot of that corporate issuance, I would say, is almost yield-agnostic, because the build-out for AI, the returns on that, the companies believe they're going to be so high. They don't really care what they're paying," he said recently.

U.S. investment-grade corporate bond issuance totaled about $1.7 trillion in the year to date through July, about 27% above last year's pace and on track to exceed $2 trillion for the first time, according to Wall Street veteran Ed Yardeni.

A flood of corporate debt that massive would typically require yields to offer a bigger premium over risk-free bonds in order to attract enough buyers.

But in the case of AI-related bonds, demand has been so high that the yield spread has remained compressed, barely widening for an additional premium, he pointed out in a note on Monday.

"As a result, the market has adjusted not through higher corporate borrowing costs relative to Treasuries but through higher Treasury yields themselves. Capital flowing into corporate bonds is capital not flowing into Treasuries, and Treasury yields have had to rise to clear the market," Yardeni explained. "In short, the AI revolution is producing a classic crowding-out effect, causing Treasury yields to rise."

Higher yields could eventually fuel a feedback loop where rising debt-servicing costs expand deficits further and further add on to the pile of U.S. debt, which in turn pushes yields up further.

To be sure, the rise in Treasury yields has been attributed to a variety factors, in addition to the AI debt orgy. They include massive federal budget deficits with no end in sight, higher oil prices due to the Iran war, and a robust U.S. economy continuing to put upward pressure on inflation.

title: El-Sayed apologizes for comments he made responding to an attack on a Michigan synagogue
description: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, apologized to the state's Jewish Democratic Caucus on Saturday for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which h...
fullText:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, apologized to the state's Jewish Democratic Caucus on Saturday for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which he tied to Israel's actions in the Middle East.

"My comments may have been misconstrued to justify something I did not mean to justify," El-Sayed told reporters after he addressed the caucus at a party convention in Lansing. "To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry. That was not my intention."

El-Sayed's apology was his latest attempt to unify Democrats after a bitter primary where he defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. He's eager to push past a series of controversies involving allegations of antisemitism, including his association with controversial commentator Hasan Piker. He faces Republican nominee Mike Rogers in a race that will help determine control of the Senate.

In March, a man attacked Temple Israel synagogue in a Detroit suburb, ramming his car into the building and opening fire on a security guard before dying by suicide. The man, Ayman Mohammad Ghazali, had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week prior.

In a video response at the time, El-Sayed condemned the attack and added that "hurt people hurt people," a reference to what happened to Ghazali's family. Critics accused El-Sayed of justifying Ghazali's actions.

"What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn't the time for context," El-Sayed said on Saturday, "and you don't ever want to trample somebody's pain."

Viktor Hovland will head into the final round of the PGA Tour's $40m Tour Championship in Atlanta on Sunday with a one-stroke lead.

The season-ending event will also crown the FedEx Cup champion, which was won by Hovland in 2023.

The Norwegian, who came into the third round tied for the lead on 10 under with American Ryan Gerard, birdied the 17th and 18th holes to post a five-under-par 65 to improve to 15 under.

Gerard also birdied the final hole to finish one back on 14 under after a round of 66.

Lurking in the chasing pack are the world's top two players, with number one Scottie Scheffler, the 2024 champion, producing a serene bogey-free round of 66 to finish three adrift on 12 under.

Back-to-back Masters champion Rory McIlroy - a record three-time FedEx Cup winner in 2016, 2019 and 2022 - catapulted himself into contention with a hugely impressive 63 to sit five shots off the lead.

The 37-year-old found form with his putter as he holed nine birdies, including three in a row on 15, 16 and 17 to post the joint lowest round of the day.

"I just left myself in better spots on the greens," said McIlroy.

"I gave myself easier putts, putts that didn't break two ways. When I got it rolling there on the back nine, every putt was like a cup right or a cup left."

Australia's Adam Scott, 46, who won the Tour Championship 20 years ago is alongside Scheffler after also carding a 66, while Sweden's Ludvig Aberg posted a 65 to also finish on 12 under.

McIlroy is joined on 10 under by Players Championship winner Cameron Young.

England's Justin Rose and Matt Fitzpatrick are probably too far back to challenge or the title at eight under par.

title: 'Not bad for the worst team in Premier League history' - Hull's perfect start
description: Hull striker Oli McBurnie has a playful dig at his team's critics after beating Coventry to win their opening two Premier League games.
fullText:
"To say we're the worst team in Premier League history, it's not a bad start from the boys," said Ollie McBurnie, in a light-hearted jab to Hull's critics.

Liam Millar's late winner at Coventry made it two wins from two to leave the Tigers in dreamland on their Premier League return.

After the opening day victory over Manchester United it was a different, gritty, display on Saturday but winning at CBS Arena, against a perceived relegation rival, earns Hull huge momentum and belief.

"We don't feel we have anything to prove to anyone. No-one has given us the Premier League, we have all earned it," said striker McBurnie.

"We're there on merit, we deserve to be there, we don't have anything to prove to anyone. It's been a great start."

The Scotland international refused to get carried away but the tune of "we're going to win the league" from the away end signalled the Hull fans' glee.

It may be fanciful but at least history is on the Tigers' side as they look to stay in the division.

Only three teams have ever been relegated from the top flight having won their first two games.

One was the Tigers themselves in 2016-17. Wolves in 2011-12 and West Brom in 2017-18 are the others.

Their Premier League survival chances were written off instantly after beating Middlesbrough in the Championship play-off final last season. They now sit second in the early table.

At Coventry, Hull looked built for the Premier League. Hulking defender Semi Ajayi dominated at the heart of the Tigers' defence to limit the Sky Blues, who ultimately ran out of ideas.

Nobel Mendy and Lucas Gourna-Douath towered above the hosts while McBurnie was a constant nuisance.

The Tigers are the first promoted side to win their opening two games for nine years, since Huddersfield dispatched Crystal Palace and Newcastle.

The Terriers beat the drop by four points in 2017-18 and that remains the goal for boss Sergej Jakirovic, especially after his men struggled to find inspiration at Coventry until Millar's intervention.

Prior to the substitute's winner there was frustration pouring out of Mendy when Hull's record signing threw his hands in the air and pulled his shirt over his head after being withdrawn on the hour.

The Sky Blues had almost 70% possession but were unable to break Hull down - and as Coventry's agitation grew so did the Tigers' belief.

"The longer the game was 0-0 the pressure was more on them to win the game. A draw was not a bad result for us," added McBurnie.

For Coventry, after 25 years away it was not supposed to start like this.

All the anticipation, all the waiting and it ends with a crushing dose of reality.

A second successive defeat will serve as a reminder that, despite the euphoria of their top-flight return, this season will be a constant battle.

Coventry can at least seek solace in the fact 10 promoted sides have lost their first two Premier League games and survived, the last being Aston Villa in 2019-20.

But they will need to improve. Having scored 97 goals in winning the title last season they must rediscover that touch, although they are not helped by Haji Wright's thigh injury which will keep him sidelined for weeks.

When the fixtures came out, though, a home game with fellow promoted side Hull stood out as one to get early points.

Sandwiched between an opener at champions Arsenal and a trip to runners-up Manchester City the Sky Blues needed to take something.

Yet owner Doug King looked on grimly from the stands as he watched time tick by and the Sky Blues fail to recover from Millar's 82nd-minute strike.

The opening 3-0 defeat at Arsenal was understandable but this defeat leaves them already playing catch up.

They were persistent but limited, with seven of the starting XI remaining from the 0-0 draw against Hull which opened last season's Championship campaign.

There was a nervousness about the Sky Blues, which was picked up by boss Frank Lampard. It is something which needs eradicating quickly.

"This season was always going to be very different to last season but I sensed a bit of edge, that quality of pass and playing safe rather than play forward," he said. "Maybe that is apprehension.

"I don't like the excuse of it. Last week that was valid because of the level of opposition, the occasion, 25 years out and a lot of debuts. We shouldn't use it as an excuse today.

"It's a game against a team we played twice last year and we finished a lot of points above them. The Premier League gives that edge and we will have to get used to that and quickly.

"The lesson is don't expect anything in the Premier League. It depends how much you want it to be (a mental blow). There are 36 games left, we're two games in. It depends how you want to react to defeats."

Ashley Williams believes the defeat will hit Coventry's confidence.

The former Wales captain won promotion to the Premier League with Swansea in 2011 and knows how crucial the early psychological blows can be.

"They blitzed the Championship last year and were full of confidence coming into the season. But after two defeats everything suddenly becomes that much harder," he said on the BBC's Final Score programme.

"As players, you look at the table and it's not nice when you are at the wrong end of it. Straight away they'll see they are already six points behind Hull and that's a real kick in the teeth.

"All those little doubts start to kick in so they've got to get to work and figure it out fast and I'm sure Frank Lampard will do that. However, Manchester City away next up is far from ideal."

title: Newcastle show there's plenty of life after Tonali
description: Newcastle United sold Sandro Tonali to Tottenham Hotspur, but the club look to have reinvested the money wisely following United's 2-0 win in north London.
fullText:
Sandro Tonali anticipated being "more nervous" than usual about coming up against former club Newcastle United for the first time.

You suspect the Tottenham Hotspur midfielder felt a little sick following their 2-0 defeat on Saturday evening.

"Sandro, what's the score?" the away fans taunted in the closing stages as the substituted Italian looked on.

This bruising loss was certainly not the reunion Tonali had in mind after joining Spurs for a fee worth up to £100m last month.

It is still very early days, of course, but Newcastle appear to have reinvested the money wisely after spending a similar combined amount on midfielder Nico Gonzalez, defender Amar Dedic and goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek.

A number of the players head coach Matthias Jaissle inherited, such as goalscorers Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa, also look reborn.

Yet he was rightly not getting carried away following his first Premier League win.

"We have our own goals and we are clear with that," Jaissle said. "We are also realistic. Now you write everything is top, everything is great.

"We don't follow that too much. We are emotionally very stable and don't see the highs higher than it is now.

"It is a moment to enjoy as well after that start, but we are also smart enough to see a long journey ahead of us and there will be challenges as well."

Jaissle, by his own admission, "likes challenges" and this was certainly a big one to take on.

It is exactly 30 days since predecessor Eddie Howe oversaw what proved to be his final match in charge, a sobering 4-1 friendly defeat against Bristol City, before stepping down.

Newcastle had sold Tonali. Anthony Gordon had left for Barcelona. Captain Bruno Guimaraes' sights were set on a move to Arsenal.

The start of the season was also rapidly approaching.

Newcastle have made further additions since then, but only one of their seven summer signings, Gonzalez, has previously played in the Premier League.

All of the new arrivals are aged 24 and under.

Yet you would not necessarily know it by the immediate impact full-back Dedic has made following his £30m move from Benfica, or how Hornicek has stood up to the physicality of the Premier League since his £25.7m switch from Braga.

It could easily be forgotten, given what happened after the break at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, but Hornicek was among those to play an important role in this win after making three saves at crucial moments in the first half.

No wonder Jaissle clenched his fists on the touchline after Hornicek got a strong hand behind Jan Paul van Hecke's header.

There was a similarly enthusiastic reaction from the former Hoffenheim defender when Lewis Hall blocked a goalbound effort from Pedro Porro in the first half.

"In the first half, we didn't play a really good game, but we could really count on everyone throwing everything into every ball and every cross," Jaissle said.

"This is the commitment and belief that we can keep the clean sheet, so that makes me proud."

Although Newcastle defeated Spurs last season, too, there were also a number of games when the visitors wilted in such circumstances.

Newcastle won just four of their 19 top-flight matches on the road and, home or away, they had not previously kept a single clean sheet since March.

However, going in level in their first away day of this campaign gave Newcastle the chance to regroup at half-time.

The visitors sought to be more aggressive after the break and clinically took Spurs apart with their only two shots on target.

For the first, just as he did in the opening stages, new signing Gonzalez hit a stunning cross field ball over the head of Spurs left-back Andy Robertson for the advancing Dedic to flick on to Elanga, who turned Tonali inside the box and fired the ball in off the post.

"It is something that I spoke about with the coach, even before the game," Gonzalez said.

"He wanted me to see these kind of balls and I tried a few in the first half and the second half, and we scored.

"In the second half we said, 'we have to keep doing this' because it is really hard to defend players like Amar, a full-back that comes this fast from behind. Normally wingers don't defend these kind of balls very well.

"It's something that we have to keep doing and I hope it gives us many more goals this season."

For Newcastle's second, Sean Steur's corner was headed down by fellow substitute Nick Woltemade and Wissa improvised with a clever overhead kick to double his side's lead.

For all the focus on Newcastle's new arrivals, it was rather fitting that two players who endured difficult first seasons at the club stepped up under Jaissle once again as Elanga and Wissa built on improved showings against Liverpool on the opening weekend.

"He's a really dynamic manager so we need to give everything," Wissa told Sky Sports. "I think he's the best signing."

title: Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight

Filip Hrgovic ripped up the script and shattered Moses Itauma's world-title dream as the Briton appeared to punch himself out in an extraordinary heavyweight contest in London.

Itauma, 21, controlled most of the fight and scored a second-round knockdown but faded as his relentless output caught up with him.

Hrgovic weathered the storm and piled on the pressure in the ninth. With Itauma barely able to stand, his legs unsteady and body swaying before slumping in the corner, his team threw in the towel.

Itauma - who needed medical attention before leaving the arena on a stretcher - had been a heavy favourite after tearing through his first 14 opponents and was spoken about as heavyweight boxing's next superstar.

"He is the best I have been in the ring with, but he needs more experience. I knew I was losing the round, but I knew that I had the pace in my favour. He needs more experience, but he is one of a kind," Hrgovic said.

"From the first round, I saw his gassing out. He started fast. I knew he was going to gas out. I knew when my chance came I needed to push. That is what I did."

With the vacant IBF title on the line, victory would have made Itauma the second-youngest world champion in the division's history.

Instead, his inexperience began to show as his Croatian opponent - an Olympic bronze medallist whose only previous professional defeat came against Daniel Dubois - survived everything Itauma threw at him before completing a remarkable turnaround.

Wardley-Dubois rematch set for 17 October in London

Relive Hrgovic's dramatic stoppage win over Itauma to claim IBF heavyweight title - reaction

Cameron beats Mayer to become unified light-middleweight champion

Hrgovic - wearing the red and white checks of his country - made his entrance first to a wall of boos, before the mood inside the O2 Arena flipped as Itauma emerged to a huge roar - taking his time and soaking up the reception.

The crowd had made its allegiances clear after a fiery build-up which included Itauma shoving Hrgovic, the Zagreb man slapping him back and plenty of verbal sparring.

Itauma came out with real intent, landing straight lefts from his southpaw stance. Hrgovic is known for his durability but struggled to keep pace with the Briton's speed early on.

Early in the second, a right hook knocked Hrgovic off-balance and his glove touched the canvas. Oasis star Noel Gallagher and boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed were among those watching as the crowd gasped at almost every Itauma punch, whether it landed or not.

But by the end of the third, Itauma - who had boxed just 26 professional rounds before his first world-title fight - was already breathing heavily.

There had also been questions over his chin, simply because it had never really been tested. Hrgovic began landing the occasional heavy shot but Itauma took them well and fired straight back.

A fight in the crowd momentarily took attention away from the action in the fifth before an Itauma uppercut in the closing seconds brought the focus back to the ring.

Itauma continued to fire combinations but Hrgovic was barely budging. A huge right landed on the bell in the sixth and another followed in the seventh, yet the Croatian simply walked through them.

The Briton was well ahead but, rather than box his way towards victory, he continued to chase the knockout. A flurry in the eighth backed Hrgovic on to the ropes and had him in trouble, but Itauma was grimacing between exchanges and looking increasingly spent.

The youngster somehow stayed upright but his legs had gone. Hrgovic continued to press and when Itauma slumped into his corner, exhausted and barely able to defend himself, referee Howard Foster waved off the contest as the towel came in.

Hrgovic admitted he had been "outboxed" but leaves London as Croatia's first heavyweight world champion, with Frank Sanchez waiting as the IBF mandatory challenger.

A unification fight could follow, with Daniel Dubois holding the WBO title and set to face Fabio Wardley again in October.

For Itauma, this was supposed to be a coronation.

Instead, he leaves the O2 Arena with questions over whether the step up came too soon.

He has time to rebuild and there will be a strong feeling that, with a little more experience, this night could have ended very differently.

Londoner Dubois was stopped by Joe Joyce as an unbeaten 23-year-old before going on to become a two-time world champion. Itauma has even more time on his side.

"He's an amazing fighter," Hrgovic said. "I am the present. He is definitely the future."

Promoter Frank Warren suggested Itauma was carrying a leg injury in the final round but backed him to return.

"Moses gave everything," he added. "He has to go back to the drawing board and he can come again."

The expectation around Itauma will not disappear entirely overnight but the aura of invincibility has gone.

title: Cameron beats Mayer to become unified light-middleweight champion
description: Chantelle Cameron produced one of the finest displays of her career to beat Mikaela Mayer and add the WBA and WBC light-middleweight titles to her WBO belt.
fullText:
Chantelle Cameron produced one of the finest displays of her career to beat Mikaela Mayer and add the WBA and WBC light-middleweight titles to her WBO belt.

An engrossing encounter was narrowly won by the British fighter by unanimous decision - 97-93 on two scorecards and 96-94 on the other.

American Mayer disagreed with the decision, claiming she "outboxed" Cameron – leading to an angry exchange of words in the ring.

The possibility of a rematch was also floated, with Mayer suggesting Cameron had benefited from home advantage – to the champion's chagrin, as she said "talk is cheap".

It means Cameron remains unbeaten since her second fight with Katie Taylor in 2023, and with 23 victories in 24 professional encounters.

Relive Hrgovic's dramatic stoppage win over Itauma to claim IBF heavyweight title

Dubois beats Moore to keep Baumgardner in picture

Itauma punches himself out against Hrgovic in world-title fight

This was one of Cameron's best displays. These fighters were evenly matched in every metric – from punch rate to height and weight, even hairstyle.

But Cameron won out thanks to her unrelenting pressure, which never allowed the usually adaptable Mayer to figure out a winning gameplan.

Mayer was the more imposing figure early on, but Cameron played counterpuncher until she could get onto the front foot.

Cameron forced Mayer against the ropes in round four, and again at the start of the fifth. Increasingly confident to take the initiative, she was roared on by a partisan but disappointingly small home crowd.

Mayer was unable to get in behind her jab for long periods and was bleeding and breathing heavily by round six.

The home favourite was cut in the final rounds but pushed through and was lifted shoulder high by her team before her biggest win since beating Taylor in Dublin three years ago was announced.

For three-weight world champion Mayer, this is the third defeat of her 25-fight career and costs her the WBA and WBC belts, which Cameron now puts with her WBO title.

When this event was announced, it was the prime event of the August bank holiday weekend in British boxing.

However, the elevation of Moses Itauma v Filip Hrgovic to a world title fight left this big-ticket event feeling rather undeservedly like a support act.

That was reflected in the crowd, with scores of empty seats around the arena as the main undercard began. At a generous estimate, BP Pulse Arena was half-full when the fighters made their ring walks for the main event.

Mayer and Cameron did their best to bring the big fight feeling in the build-up. Previously cordial relations boiled over on Friday as they butted heads at Friday's weigh-in at BP Pulse Arena.

Cameron shoved her head into the American, who pushed back, before they exchanged insults side by side.

On fight night, Mayer played up her away status by entering the ring to American Woman by Lenny Kravitz. She also wore a black durag over her trademark blonde hair, before removing it to show tight dreadlocks – the same style as Cameron.

However, her moxie was eventually worn down by Cameron, with a big right to the chin in round seven the most notable of blows.

This fight headlined the event marking the fifth anniversary of Most Valuable Promotions (MVP), the promoters fronted by Jake Paul who, since 2021, have moved from YouTuber fights to leading the way for women's boxing in the UK.

Paul, influencer and co-founder of MVP, was in the house. He headlined on 29 August 2021, beating MMA fighter Tyron Woodley, but was in a watching brief here.

MVP's next women's boxing arena event will take place in November in Texas.

It will be headlined by unified super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner, with the American stepping up to lightweight to face IBF champion Elif Nur Turhan – on her way to a potential 2027 showdown with WBC and WBO champion Caroline Dubois.

World championship fights on the undercard will include featherweight champion Tiara Brown defending against former super-bantamweight undisputed champion Ellie Scotney, and super-bantamweight champion Skye Nicolson against three-time, two-division champion Miyo Yoshida.

The next fight is particularly important for Cameron, after her first bout at BP Pulse Arena since November 2024 – and first since her much-lauded move to MVP.

MVP have plenty of options they could introduce from their stable. IBF light-middleweight champion Oshae Jones seems the logical next step; or IBF, WBO and The Ring middleweight belt holder Tammara Thibeault of Canada.

Cameron regularly laments that she has not had the chances her talent deserves since her blockbuster double header against Taylor in 2023.

Three years on, she will want fights of that level – especially after Saturday night's result.

title: £300m spent, bottom of the table... but Spurs boss De Zerbi 'not angry'
description: Having spent more than £300m in the summer, Tottenham find themselves bottom of the Premier League, without a point or a goal, but boss Roberto de Zerbi remains optimistic.
fullText:
Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi said he was "not angry" and there was "no panic" after his side's second loss in two games left them bottom of the Premier League – but it was a depressingly familiar story for the club's fans.

Goals from Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa in a 10-minute second-half spell gave Newcastle a 2-0 victory, with thousands of Spurs supporters heading for the exits early.

They have every reason to be annoyed as they have now seen only three home league wins from their past 23 matches at their superb stadium.

Seventeenth in the Premier League in 2024-25, 17th in 2025-26, only avoiding relegation on the final day, but this season was meant to be different.

With more than £300m spent in the summer, Spurs fans were expecting a push to get back into Europe, having won the Europa League two seasons ago and been in the last 16 of the Champions League in March.

Instead, in the Premier League it is played two, lost two, scored none, 20th out of 20.

"We can improve in the defensive phases but today was an unfair result," said De Zerbi.

"Disappointed for the result because until the first goal we conceded, we played better than Newcastle.

"We are disappointed for the result and [for] our fans. We are working to be a great team. When we become a team, we can change the story of the last two seasons for Tottenham."

After beating Everton on the final day of last season to stay up, Tottenham tried to ensure they were not in a relegation scrap this year.

In came midfielders Mateus Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £85m and £100m respectively, defender Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton for £52m and Manchester City winger Savio, formerly known as Savinho, for £75m, although he missed Saturday's match because of "muscle fatigue".

Defenders Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson, plus goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, have arrived on free transfers and striker Omar Marmoush made his debut against Newcastle following his loan from Manchester City, with the deal becoming a permanent £60m transfer next summer.

After a 3-0 loss at Brentford last week, more home pain was inflicted on the Spurs support, although the Magpies scored with both of their attempts on target as Tottenham failed to convert any of their 17 attempts, six of which were on target.

"Forget the result," insisted De Zerbi. "I am not angry, we are working well and were unlucky today with the result.

"There is no panic. I know where we are going and what the plan is. I'm sorry for the fans for the result. We have to improve. We have to work hard on the pitch and find the connection between the players."

Former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Joe Hart was not as positive about Spurs' performances and said: "The frustration in the stadium, and among the fans, will be they are looking at that Spurs team and wondering what they are trying to achieve.

"When you see a Newcastle side who have been through massive change over the summer - and a more difficult change than Spurs have - it's hard as in two games you can clearly see what [Newcastle boss] Matthias Jaissle is trying to do. The players are on board with it and they are flying.

"The concern for Tottenham is they can't say the same. But there's been a lot of change and it's not easy to bed in that many players under so much pressure.

"Hardly anyone has been able to find the remedy at the club so it's not like it's an easy fix. They've not just suddenly fallen off a cliff, they've been struggling in the league for a while.

"Roberto de Zerbi needs to get his new players to settle in quickly as the Premier League comes at you so fast, and it feels like his team are second-guessing everything at the moment."

Former England goalkeeper Rob Green, speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, added: "Lukas Hornicek made some saves in the first half but Tottenham were short of invention, creation, goals.

"For Tottenham, the same questions last season are still here this season. Performances like this will indicate that they need a vast improvement from this set of players that have come into this club.

"They will need the characters as much as anything to turn this around. It doesn't take much for these Spurs fans to turn and the belief start to drain from the players."

The transfer window closes on Tuesday, and on Friday De Zerbi said he was still seeking "one player 

After the Newcastle match he was asked about the potential departures of Kevin Danso, Pape Matar Sarr and Richarlison, who have all been linked with moves away from Tottenham.

"I have very good relationships but if they want to leave, they have to bring the solution, the economic solution, to the club, and they can go," he said.

De Zerbi was only appointed at the end of March, earning 11 points in seven matches to keep Spurs up, and insists it will not be a quick fix to the club's problems.

"We have to improve and to change two seasons like the last two is impossible in 10 days and with people in the transfer market," said the Italian.

"We have to work hard on the pitch and find the connection with the players because last season before the end of the season we were in the Championship and we stayed up together.

"Now we have to keep calm and focus on improvement. We have a great squad and great players."

title: GB's Fery beaten in his first ATP Tour final
description: Arthur Fery misses out on his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat by Ignacio Buse in the final of the Winston-Salem Open.
fullText:
Arthur Fery missed out on his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat by Ignacio Buse in the final of the Winston-Salem Open.

Fery, who was the talk of Wimbledon as he reached the semi-finals of his home major in July, lost 6-3 6-2 to Peru's Buse.

The 24-year-old was the first Briton to reach the final of the ATP 250 tournament in North Carolina and will rise to 33 in the world rankings as a result - overtaking Cameron Norrie as British number one.

Only eight weeks ago, before his astonishing run to the last four at the All England Club, he was ranked outside the top 100.

Little could separate Fery and Buse in the early stages of their match on Saturday, before the Peruvian took control with a break to love for a 5-3 lead.

Fery quickly fell further behind in the second set as Buse opened up a double break cushion with no reply, and while he pulled back one of those breaks, it proved to no avail as his opponent reeled off three straight games to seal the win.

For 22-year-old Buse, victory makes him the youngest ever winner of Winston-Salem and marks a second career title after he beat American Tommy Paul at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg in May.

With little time to reflect on his Winston-Salem run, Fery will now head to New York for the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Set to play at Flushing Meadows for the first time, he faces a tough opening tie against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Fery is one of nine British players set to feature in the main draws at the US Open, the final Grand Slam of the season.

Joining him in the men's draw are Norrie and Jan Choinski, qualifiers Toby Samuel and Harry Wendelken, and lucky loser Jacob Fearnley.

Katie Boulter is joined by qualifiers Fran Jones and Harriet Dart in the women's draw, but both Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu are missing through injury.

title: Decision to curtail play at Lord's 'a joke' - Hussain
description: The decision to abandon play an hour early after a rain-hit third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan is criticised by former captain Nasser Hussain and fans.
fullText:
The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nasser Hussain.

On a Saturday badly affected by persistent showers at Lord's, players left the field at 17:08 BST.

At that point, prospects of conditions improving sufficiently for play to resume seemed remote. However, rain cleared and the sky brightened.

The groundstaff partially removed the covers while officials deliberated. At 18:30, with up to an hour of playing time remaining and with the weather the best it had been all day, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned proceedings.

The decision was greeted with booing by some of the sparse crowd that remained inside the ground.

"That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports.

"I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is.

"In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."

The weather stayed dry and the light remained good up to 19:30, the time at which play would have been scheduled to close.

The morning session had been washed out and only 24.5 overs of play were possible as the players dodged the showers, meaning spectators will receive a 50% refund on the price of their ticket.

If 30 overs had been completed, spectators would not have been entitled to any money back.

Still, the abandonment caused some fans to express their displeasure with messages to the BBC's live coverage of the Test.

"Sat in the Edrich Stand," wrote Joe at Lord's. "It hasn't rained for half an hour and it's as bright as it's been all day. Absolutely no justification for not playing right now. A real shame."

Rachel in Kingswinford added: "Ridiculous to call it off! They want fans supporting Test cricket and those spectators have stuck with it all day - another 30-45 mins of play would have been a better look (plus saving authorities money on refunds)!"

Another message from Paul in Northwich read: "This is a terrible advert for cricket. It's like the umpires are waiting for it to rain again. At least the spectators can get a refund."

Vaughan backs Lawrence for extended run in England team

Lawrence impresses as weather delays England

Play ended with England 177-7 in their second innings, 357 ahead and on course to win the match and series.

Batting conditions had been difficult all day and it would have been another challenging period for the home side had they been asked to return for a short time late in the evening.

"It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50.

"It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward.

"Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."

The situation at Lord's came on the same day Durham were denied the chance to chase a victory target of four against Gloucestershire because of bad light at the end of the third day of their County Championship match at Chester-le-Street.

It means the teams will return on Sunday for what could be as little as one ball of action.

Gloucestershire were dismissed for 250 in their second innings in the closing stages of Saturday, with visiting coach Mark Alleyne claiming the light was already too poor before his team were all out.

"I'm not sure where to start, really," said Alleyne. "I mean, 45 minutes before we lost the last wicket, it was too dark to play, which would have been consistent with all the other days that we played."

"We had probably 50 minutes of cricket there that we probably shouldn't have done."

The match could have been concluded had Gloucestershire chosen to bowl spin, only for the away side to refuse and push the game into a Sunday when rain is forecast.

"They asked if we would bowl our spinners to finish the game," added Alleyne. "Of course, we said no, we'll bowl our quick bowlers, in which case it became bad light, so we'll come back tomorrow."

Durham coach Ryan Campbell wrote on X: "Cricket sometimes doesn't help itself. Before everyone loads up on the poor old umpires, it's not their fault."

title: Europe's summer drought threatens fish in rivers, lakes and farms
description: Small boats stand idle on cracked ground in a shriveled side channel of the Danube River in northern Serbia, where the water has receded into a couple of shrinking ponds under pressure from extreme dr...
fullText:
NOVI SAD, Serbia (AP) — Small boats stand idle on cracked ground in a shriveled side channel of the Danube River in northern Serbia, where the water has receded into a couple of shrinking ponds under pressure from extreme drought and heat. Fish circle in the shallow waters.

"This is all we have, these two little ponds that are full of juvenile fish," fisherman Dusan Jovanovic said. He said the fish are in danger because there is too little water and its temperature is over 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).

"If they start to die, they will all die at once," Jovanovic said.

Persistent drought and scorching heat this summer have ravaged ecosystems and businesses across the region, from a lake in Slovenia and the side channel of the Danube in Serbia, to fish farms in Bosnia, the Czech Republic, Romania and Hungary.

The fish industry has been hit especially hard, with damage estimated in the millions of euros (dollars). This is adding to the already high toll caused by problems with energy and water supplies, devastated crops, losses in river traffic and trade.

Finding themselves unprepared for this year's crisis, countries and businesses are now pondering ways to minimize the effects of future extreme weather events that scientists have tied to human-induced climate change.

Around 99% of Hungary's lands are currently under severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the national meteorological service. Desertification, a process where vegetation recedes because of high heat and low rainfall, threatens much of the Great Hungarian Plain.

Among the most affected are Hungary's roughly 27,000 hectares (67,000 acres) of fish ponds. The country's Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said last week that "persistent heat and water shortages" had led to 1,588 hectares (3,924 acres) of those ponds drying out, causing the deaths of nearly 280 metric tons of fish at 20 farms.

The estimated revenue loss from the damage was 1.3 billion forints ($4.2 million), the ministry said. Producers say replacing lost fish could take years. Sometimes, operators were forced to drain one pond and divert its water to save fish in another, the Hungarian Aquaculture and Fisheries Inter-branch Organization said in early August.

For fish farmers in Romania, especially those cultivating carp, this year's blistering heatwave follows severe droughts in 2023 and 2024, the effects of which are still being felt, says Catalin Platon, president of ROMFISH National Association of Fish Producers.

In carp production, Platon said, the production cycle is three or four years.

"So what we lost in 2023 has (had an) impact every year since," he explained. Water-use policies that prioritized irrigation for agriculture during the previous droughts, "left us with no water for the fish," Platon complained.

Fish farmers across the Czech Republic have taken various emergency measures: reducing or suspending feeding to reduce oxygen use, aerating the ponds or draining them when necessary.

The Czech Fishing Association officials say sustained rainfall could ease the immediate crisis, but long-term measures are needed to retain more water in the landscape.

Jan Sokolik, a technician at the Rybarstvi Trebon fishery, explained that "some ponds that were actually low on water have already been fished, but they were all marginal ponds."

"Now we're just starting to plan what to do with the big ponds," he said.

Veljko Budjen owns a trout farm near Trebinje in southeast Bosnia. He said hot and dry summers have brought serious problems in the mainly mountainous country famous for its trout restaurants.

"Trout is a cold water fish, which requires cold water with a lot of oxygen," he said. "So during the summer you are forced to reduce trout production and feeding so the business can just barely survive."

One option, he said, is to add liquid oxygen to the water during summer months. Otherwise, he said, "you wait for the first rain."

Emergency teams have been pumping water into Lake Pristava in eastern Slovenia, a favorite spot for fishermen, to try to prevent a mass suffocation of fish from lack of oxygen and water chestnut overgrowing to cover the lake surface.

Firefighters have pumped in 8 million liters (2 million gallons) of water but they still fear it's not enough.

"We are surprised that any fish has survived at all," Danijel Fras, from the Pesnica Lenart Fishing Association, told public broadcaster RTV Slovenia.

In Serbia, fishermen said the only solution for the endangered fish in the Danube side channel in Novi Sad is to move them to another location.

"The temperatures this year are extreme," Jovanovic, the Serbian fisherman, said. "No one can remember anything like this."

Justin Spike in Budapest, Hungary, Eldar Emric in Trebinje, Bosnia, Stanislav Hodina in Prague and Steven McGrath in Leamington Spa, England, contributed.

title: Men are skipping showers before dates for a reason that may surprise women
description: Pheromone-maxxing has men skipping showers and deodorant before dates, but the science behind natural body odor and attraction remains inconclusive.
fullText:
As if dating weren't already enough of a gamble, a new trend has some men skipping their usual hygiene routines before meeting a prospective partner.

So-called "pheromone-maxxing" is a viral TikTok trend primarily associated with teen boys and young men that involves skipping showers and deodorant before a date.

Some proponents go so far as to wear unwashed shirts or drink their own urine in an effort to "sweat out toxins," Vice reported.

'Looksmaxxing' Trend Has Young Men Taking Hammers To Their Faces In Pursuit Of Sharper Features

Pheromones are chemical compounds that transmit signals between members of the same species. They are well documented in insects and other animals, and some pheromones do not have a discernible scent, Scientific American explained.

The theory behind pheromone-maxxing is that the stronger a man's natural musk, the more sexually attractive he is.

The scientific evidence behind that idea, however, is inconclusive.

Researchers have found evidence that human body odors and secretions can influence physiological or psychological responses in other people.

"But there is no evidence of a consistent and strong behavioral response to any human-produced chemical cue," Scientific American reported. "To date, scientists have collected evidence for possible pheromone effects but have not definitively identified a single human pheromone."

One of the best-known experiments examining scent and attraction was a 1995 study commonly called the "sweaty T-shirt study."

Click Here For More Lifestyle News

Male participants wore the same T-shirt for two consecutive nights, after which female participants were asked to rate the odors of six shirts.

Women generally rated the body odors of men whose MHC (major histocompatibility complex) genes differed from their own as more pleasant than those of men with more similar MHC genes. The MHC is a group of genes that plays a key role in the immune system and may also influence individual body odor.

Among women taking oral contraceptives, however, that preference was reversed.

Later research has produced mixed results.

A 2019 study of 883 couples found that people from the Netherlands and Northern Europe were more likely to choose partners with different MHC genes. Researchers did not find the same pattern among Israeli couples and suggested a history of arranged marriages in some groups could help explain why.

A 2020 analysis of previous studies, however, found no strong evidence that people prefer partners with different MHC genes or find their body odor more attractive.

Pheromone-maxxing is tied to the broader "looksmaxxing" movement, in which social media users attempt to optimize their appearance and attractiveness, sometimes through extreme measures such as cosmetic procedures and drastic diets.

Pheromone-maxxing has been making recent headlines, but the concept has circulated online since at least 2024.

A thread that year in the r/TikTokCringe subreddit drew a largely repulsed response.

"And how are those natural pheromones helping him in real life human social interactions?" one Redditor wondered.

"I am confused," commented another. "Does he think that bathing means you no longer make pheromones? Is nobody able to teach him?"

"There's no way in hell I would let my child go to school or even in my house smelling stinky," another user wrote. "It's actually sad that no one in his life has taught him the importance of cleanliness."

Discussing the trend on Fox News' "The Five," co-host Jesse Watters said, "I'm anti-cologne."

He recommended a simple pre-date shower with bar soap and shampoo.

Panelist Tyrus agreed and urged men to use unscented deodorant.

"If men put too much cologne on, you're a creep," he said. "You're sending the wrong message. You don't want to smell like gym class, but you also don't want to smell like you're cheap."

title: James Carville predicts a 2028 'reckoning' as socialist candidates eye the Democratic ticket
description: James Carville says Democratic voters won't nominate a DSA-aligned candidate in 2028, even as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez renews her membership.
fullText:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville said the Democratic Party faces an ideological "reckoning" in 2028 but rejected the idea that primary voters will choose a democratic socialist presidential nominee.

Speaking on "Saturday in America," Carville offered his prediction of how Democratic voters will approach the party's 2028 presidential primary.

"The reckoning will be in a nominating process for the nominee of the Democratic Party in 2028. This has to be taken to Democratic voters," Carville said while discussing recent victories by candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

James Carville Predicts 2028 Democratic Primary Will Test True Strength Of Party's Socialist Wing

As DSA-backed candidates have won races across the country, some centrist Democrats have raised concerns about the group's growing influence. Carville argued that Democratic voters won't nominate a DSA-aligned presidential candidate in 2028.

"Let me assure you that Democratic voters are not going to nominate the DSA or anybody close to the DSA. The Democrats have never nominated the most liberal candidate, and they're not [going to] do it in 2028," he said.

Carville Says One Democratic Socialist's 'Lunacy Of The Highest Level' Policy Could Haunt Swing-state Dems

Despite Carville's prediction about 2028, several DSA-backed candidates have secured primary victories this year, with notable wins in New York and Colorado. High-profile elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, are also affiliated with the group.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., recently renewed her DSA membership after a seven-year lapse and has been discussed as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

2028 Battleground Poll Scrambles Democrats' Future As Insurgent Socialist Seizes Lead

"First of all, she has more talent than most of the people on the left put together. And I put her in an entirely different category," Carville said of Ocasio-Cortez.

title: Baby goats with rabies at North Carolina mobile petting zoo prompt calls across multiple counties to contact health officials
description: Several baby goats at a mobile petting zoo in North Carolina were infected with rabies, and authorities are asking anyone who had contact with the animals to reach out to health officials about potent...
fullText:
Multiple baby goats at a mobile petting zoo in North Carolina were infected with rabies, and authorities are asking anyone who had contact with the animals to reach out to health officials about potential exposure to the rare but deadly virus.

Residents in western North Carolina may have been exposed to the infected goats from Farm Adventures at the mobile petting zoo's location in Harmony or at off-site events between July 28 and August 27, local officials said in a statement. The state has not reported human cases of the virus since 2011.

Exposure may have happened at 10 locations, including an assisted living facility and back-to-school bash, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said. Those affected are urged to contact their local health department to determine whether they need medication to prevent infection.

The goats were most likely exposed to rabies by a skunk that had entered their pen in late July, according to the state health department, which was first notified of the rabies exposure on Thursday.

Lab testing found the virus in three of the baby goats, and a fourth is also assumed to have been infected, state officials said.

Farm Adventures is based in Iredell County and books events in surrounding communities, and officials say the owner has been cooperating with the investigation.

"There is not a broad risk to the public — only those who attended events at the mobile petting zoo and were in close contact with the goats are at risk," officials said.

"Residents should not wait for symptoms before calling," Mecklenburg County Health Director Kimberly Scott said.

Scott told CNN a coordinated statewide investigation is still seeking "specifics on total reach across counties and total number of people impacted." Communicable disease teams across multiple counties are alerting the public and working with the petting zoo to contact event organizers.

She said healthcare systems appear to have enough postexposure prophylaxis (PEP), the typical rabies treatment, available, and officials are "positioned to acquire access to more as needed as we learn more information."

"What's important is that we don't wait for the onset of symptoms when it is more difficult to treat and often most fatal," Scott said.

Farm Adventures said its "4 precious baby goats" were euthanized and its staff is "closely monitoring our remaining animals under the guidelines provided by health officials." The goats had been kept in a separate pen because they were too young for vaccinations, the petting zoo said.

"I care about my community, and I care about my customers," Misty Love, the owner of Farm Adventures, told CNN on Saturday. "If my customers that saw my animals have questions, I'm going to be there for them."

Love said a wild skunk was found in the goat enclosure on July 29, and the animal was shot and burned. The goats did not appear to have been bitten and showed no signs of rabies, according to Love. But one goat died on August 19. The next day, she said, another goat became ill and was euthanized.

A necropsy on one of the animals revealed the infection.

"RIP Molly, Maggie, cow and Uno," the zoo's post said.

Since confirming the virus, state officials say they have been working with the farm and local health departments to find out when and where residents were exposed.

Animals from the petting zoo were at the Masonic Picnic in Mocksville on August 15, according to a Facebook post from Davie County Health and Human Services. Additionally, Catawba and Burke counties said the petting zoo was at a private event near Hickory on August 9. Another event at Breeden Amphitheater in Lexington on August 1 included the petting zoo, according to the Davidson County Health Department.

Other potential exposure sites included private events in Mecklenburg, Watauga, Durham and Iredell counties, according to the state health department.

State health officials said they are working with event organizers to notify attendees who may have had contact with the infected goats.

No other animals on the farm pose a risk of rabies exposure to people, the department said.

Though human cases of rabies in the United States are rare, the disease can be deadly if people don't receive treatment before symptoms begin. Fewer than 10 deaths are reported each year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Rabies is caused by a virus that is spread mainly through the saliva of infected animals. This virus is typically transmitted through an animal bite, though scratches or direct contact with mucosa can also spread the virus.

The virus primarily affects the central nervous system, with inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. The incubation period, the time between exposure to the virus and symptom onset, can last weeks to months. Once a person starts showing symptoms of rabies, the disease is nearly always fatal.

During incubation, there are typically no symptoms. Weeks to months after exposure, an infected person may experience flu-like symptoms that can include fever, headache and overall body aches. Discomfort, such as a prickling sensation, at the site of the bite is also possible.

Rabies is preventable but requires vaccination or immediate medical attention after exposure, according to the CDC. Postexposure prophylaxis is highly effective if received soon after exposure.

Rabies transmission from livestock holds a lower risk than bites from wild animals, but people can still be exposed to the virus through saliva from an infected animal, the North Carolina health department said.

"Because baby goats are frequently bottle-fed, handled closely, or cuddled, public health officials are working proactively to ensure anyone who had direct contact with the affected animals is evaluated," the department said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Jamie Gumbrecht and Dianne Gallagher contributed to this report.

BERLIN, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Finland's President Alexander Stubb said he did not believe Russia would risk an attack against a NATO country, telling Germany's ‌Bild newspaper it would "make no sense" to test the resolve of the alliance.

Western ‌officials have warned of a growing risk of Russian hybrid operations, including cyber attacks, against European countries ​potentially leading to a direct confrontation with the NATO alliance. German officials have said they assess Russia would be in a position to attack a NATO country by 2029.

"If anyone has a crystal ball like that – that's great. I simply see neither evidence nor ‌facts to support it," he told ⁠Bild in an interview published on Saturday, adding he did not believe that Russia "would ever want to attack NATO, the world's most ⁠powerful military alliance."

Stubb, whose country joined NATO in 2023, abandoning its previous policy of neutrality following Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year earlier, said the alliance had to be prepared ​for any ​scenario but he did not believe Moscow ​was in a position to go ‌to war with NATO.

He said NATO's strength in conventional weapons, missiles and nuclear weapons was too strong to attack, adding that he had intelligence information to back his assessment.

"It makes no sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance," Stubb said.

He said Russia was trying to spread alarm in Europe through ‌its information war. But it was currently taking ​unsustainable losses in Ukraine, losing around 30,000-35,000 troops a ​month and recruiting only around ​27,000.

"So they have fewer and fewer soldiers in an increasingly complex ‌situation," he said. "I simply cannot see them ​suddenly being able to ​mobilise forces for two fronts."

Stubb said Ukraine was in a stronger position than at any time during the war, and it was vital that Europe continued ​to support Kjiv.

"We must ‌understand – you in Germany and we in Finland – that Ukraine is the best ​security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose," he ​said.
